stimuli.title: Passage I: Literary Narrative
stimuli.text:
The alarm went off at four-fifteen, and for the first eleven days Tess had lain still for a full minute afterward, listening to the house and hoping her uncle had decided not to go out. He always went out. By the twelfth morning she had stopped hoping and simply got up, pulled on the orange bib overalls that still smelled of someone else's summers, and went down to the kitchen, where Warren was already standing at the counter eating toast over the sink.

"Fog," he said, which was all the forecast she was going to get.

The Marguerite sat low at the float with the engine idling, bait barrels lashed along the rail. Tess had learned to step aboard without looking at the gap of black water, to coil a line so it ran clean, to keep her feet out of the loops when the trap went over. She had learned these things because Warren showed her once, slowly, and then did not show her again, and the second time she got it wrong he said only, "Line," and waited. Her mother called this stubbornness. Tess was beginning to think it was something else, a kind of respect that assumed you would figure it out.

They ran out past the ledges with the radar sweeping green and the shore gone entirely. Warren drove standing up, one hand on the wheel, reading the plotter like a newspaper. Tess filled bait bags at the stern table, stuffing herring into mesh and cinching the drawstrings until her hands were slick and numb. The smell no longer bothered her. That had surprised her more than anything, that something could be unbearable on a Tuesday and ordinary by Friday.

The first string of traps came up in a line of yellow and black buoys, each one appearing out of the fog a few seconds before the boat reached it. Warren gaffed the line, ran it through the hauler, and the trap rose dripping over the rail. Tess opened the door. This was the part she had dreaded at the start, reaching into the trap among the moving claws, but there was a way to do it, from behind, thumb and fingers across the back of the shell where the lobster could not get at you, and once you knew the way, the fear had nowhere to live.

She measured each one with the brass gauge, from the eye socket to the end of the carapace. Shorts went back over the side. Oversize went back too, the big breeders the law protected. Keepers she banded, slipping the thick rubber over each claw, and dropped into the tank. Warren watched the first few traps and then stopped watching, and she understood that this, too, was a kind of statement.

Near the end of the string she pulled out a female, well over the legal measure, with the tail curled under tight. She turned it over. The underside of the tail was dark with eggs, thousands of them, packed like seeds. Warren was at the wheel, his back to her, already steering for the next buoy.

Tess held the lobster for a moment. She knew the rule; she had known it since the first day, when he had explained it with the same flat patience he used for everything. An egged female went back. You cut a small notch in the tail flipper first, so that anyone who caught her later would know she was a breeder even when she was not carrying, and then she went over the side, and the fishery went on another year because of it. There was no one to see whether Tess did it. The fog was a wall on every side. Her uncle was not looking.

She reached for the notching tool on its lanyard, made the small V-shaped cut, and leaned over the rail. The lobster hung in the gray water for a second, then kicked once and was gone.

When she straightened up, Warren had not turned around. But the engine note dropped a little, as if he had eased the throttle to give her time, and she realized that he had known she would do it, had known before she did. She stacked the empty trap and reached for the next one. The fog was beginning to thin toward the east, a paler gray where the sun was, and she found that she had not thought about the time since they left the float.

stimuli.title: Passage II: Social Science
stimuli.text:
Ask a librarian what the busiest hour of the week looks like, and the answer may surprise anyone whose idea of a library was formed decades ago. At the Harlow Branch Library in a mid-sized Ohio city, the busiest hour is Tuesday at ten in the morning, when a county nurse sets up a folding table near the periodicals to take blood pressure readings, a volunteer from the legal aid society opens a laptop in the study room to help with eviction paperwork, and the children's area fills with toddlers for a bilingual story hour. Books are checked out during that hour, too. But circulation is no longer the measure by which the branch judges itself, and in that respect Harlow is typical rather than exceptional.

The shift has been under way for roughly twenty years, and it has two main sources. The first is simply demand. As other public institutions closed or shortened their hours, the library remained one of the few places that was free to enter, open to everyone, heated in winter, and staffed by people whose job was to answer questions. People brought the library the problems they could not bring anywhere else: how to apply for unemployment benefits online, where to find a notary, what to do about a letter from a collection agency. Librarians answered those questions because they were asked, and over time the answers hardened into programs.

The second source is a change in how libraries understand their mission. The profession's leading organizations now describe the library less as a collection and more as a platform, a word borrowed deliberately from the technology industry. On this view the building, the staff, and the public trust that libraries have accumulated over a century are assets that can support almost any public good: job fairs, tax preparation, seed exchanges, tool lending, passport services, citizenship classes, and, in a growing number of systems, social workers employed directly by the library to connect patrons with housing and mental health care. The Larkspur County system in Colorado hired its first full-time social worker in 2017; by 2024 it had four, and it reported that they had made more than three thousand referrals.

Measured by use, the results are striking. Program attendance at American public libraries has grown steadily even as the number of physical items checked out has declined. Surveys find that a majority of adults regard their local library as important to their community, and that the share who say so is higher among people with lower incomes. Libraries have become, in the phrase of one urban planner, the "social infrastructure" that holds neighborhoods together.

Yet the expansion has costs that its advocates do not always acknowledge. The most obvious is money. Social workers, nurses, and legal aid partnerships require budgets that most library systems were not built to carry, and funding for programs often comes out of the same line that once bought books. Between 2015 and 2023 the Harlow system's materials budget fell by nearly a fifth in real terms while its program budget more than doubled. Patrons who come for the books, a group that still includes a great many older adults and children, have noticed.

A second cost falls on the staff. Librarians are trained to find information, not to manage a mental health crisis or defuse a conflict in the reading room, and many report that the new duties arrived without new training or pay. Turnover in urban branches has risen. Some librarians say openly that they did not sign up to be the last public institution standing, and that treating the library as a safety net lets other agencies off the hook for work that is properly theirs.

A third concern is subtler. A library that offers everything to everyone risks standing for nothing in particular. The lending collection is the one service no other agency provides, and critics worry that it is being allowed to erode by neglect rather than by decision.

None of these objections has slowed the trend, and most librarians, pressed on the question, say they would not want it to. The people in line at ten on Tuesday morning are not going anywhere. But the question of what a library is for, once settled by the books on its shelves, is now open in a way it has not been for a long time, and the answer is being written branch by branch, one folding table at a time.

questions.stem: The passage is best described as the story of
options: a teenager who, over her first weeks on her uncle's boat, moves from dreading the work to taking responsibility for it on her own
a lobsterman who gradually loses patience with a niece who cannot learn the basic tasks of the boat
a girl who breaks a fishing rule to impress her uncle and is quietly caught
a family whose fishing business is threatened by new laws protecting breeding lobsters
questions.explanation: The passage opens with Tess hoping each morning that her uncle 'had decided not to go out' and ends with her notching and releasing the egg-bearing female while 'her uncle was not looking,' then realizing she 'had not thought about the time' all day. Her growth from dread to unprompted responsibility is the center of the story. Warren shows patience rather than losing it, Tess follows the rule instead of breaking it, and the law is presented as something the fishery depends on, not a threat.

questions.stem: According to the passage, on the twelfth morning Tess
options: got up without waiting to see whether her uncle would stay in
overslept and was late getting down to the float
asked Warren for a forecast and was given a detailed one
wore her own foul-weather gear for the first time
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says that for eleven days Tess lay still 'hoping her uncle had decided not to go out,' and that 'by the twelfth morning she had stopped hoping and simply got up.' The overalls she puts on 'still smelled of someone else's summers,' so they are not her own, and Warren's entire forecast is the single word 'Fog.' Nothing suggests she overslept.

questions.stem: In the third paragraph, Tess's thought that her uncle's manner is 'a kind of respect that assumed you would figure it out' most nearly suggests that she is coming to see Warren's silence as
options: a sign of confidence in her ability rather than a refusal to help
proof that he does not care whether she learns the work
the same stubbornness her mother had warned her about
a way of punishing her for the mistakes she has made
questions.explanation: The sentence directly contrasts two readings of the same behavior: her mother 'called this stubbornness,' but Tess 'was beginning to think it was something else.' Reading his silence as respect that 'assumed you would figure it out' treats it as trust in her, which the passage confirms later when Warren 'stopped watching' and she understands that as 'a kind of statement.' The stubbornness choice is the view Tess is moving away from, not toward.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the safe way to take a lobster out of a trap is to
options: grip it from behind, across the back of the shell, where the claws cannot reach
wait until the lobster has been banded before touching it
pick it up by the tail so that the claws hang downward
tip the trap over the tank so the lobster slides out on its own
questions.explanation: In the paragraph about the first string of traps, the narrator explains that 'there was a way to do it, from behind, thumb and fingers across the back of the shell where the lobster could not get at you.' Banding happens after the lobster is out and measured, and the passage describes no tail grip or tipping of the trap.

questions.stem: The statement that 'something could be unbearable on a Tuesday and ordinary by Friday' primarily serves to
options: convey how quickly Tess has adjusted to the work, in a way that surprises her
suggest that the bait smells worse on some days than on others
emphasize that Tess still finds the work nearly impossible to tolerate
explain why Warren prefers to fish early in the week
questions.explanation: The sentence follows 'The smell no longer bothered her' and 'That had surprised her more than anything.' Compressing the change into a few days of the week stresses the speed of her adjustment and her own surprise at it. The passage says the smell no longer bothers her, so it is not still unbearable, and Tuesday and Friday are used figuratively, not as a fishing schedule.

questions.stem: It can reasonably be inferred that Warren stopped watching Tess measure and band the lobsters because he
options: was satisfied that she could do the work correctly without supervision
had grown tired of correcting the same mistakes over and over
needed to concentrate on the radar as the fog grew thicker
wanted to see whether she would cut corners when unobserved
questions.explanation: Warren watches 'the first few traps and then stopped watching,' and Tess 'understood that this, too, was a kind of statement,' echoing the earlier idea that his silence is 'a kind of respect that assumed you would figure it out.' The pattern throughout the passage is that he withdraws once she is competent. Nothing says she was making mistakes at the measuring, and the later scene shows he already expected her to follow the rule rather than suspecting she would not.

questions.stem: Which detail from the passage most directly supports the idea that releasing the egg-bearing female is a test of Tess's own character rather than of her obedience?
options: the observation that no one could see whether she did it, since the fog surrounded the boat and her uncle was not looking
the explanation that an egged female is notched so later fishermen will recognize her as a breeder
the description of the eggs as 'packed like seeds' on the underside of the tail
the fact that Warren had explained the rule on the first day with his usual flat patience
questions.explanation: The passage pauses to stress that 'there was no one to see whether Tess did it,' that 'the fog was a wall on every side,' and that 'her uncle was not looking.' Those lines remove any outside pressure, so what she does next reveals her own values rather than deference to Warren. The notching explanation tells us what the rule is, and the first-day explanation tells us she knew it, but neither establishes that she is acting unobserved, which is what makes the moment a test of character.

questions.stem: According to the passage, a notch is cut in an egg-bearing female's tail flipper so that
options: anyone who catches her later will know she is a breeder even when she is not carrying eggs
the eggs will be released into the water before she is thrown back
she can be identified as belonging to Warren's traps if caught by another boat
she will no longer be able to enter a trap in the future
questions.explanation: The paragraph beginning 'Tess held the lobster' states that the notch is cut 'so that anyone who caught her later would know she was a breeder even when she was not carrying.' The notch marks the lobster for other fishermen; it does not release eggs, identify an owner, or keep the lobster out of traps.

questions.stem: The final sentence, in which Tess finds 'that she had not thought about the time since they left the float,' primarily serves to
options: mark a change in Tess from enduring the day to being absorbed by it, in contrast with the opening paragraph
suggest that Tess has lost track of how long the string of traps has taken and will be scolded
show that the fog has made it impossible to judge the hour
indicate that Warren has deliberately kept Tess too busy to notice the time
questions.explanation: The passage opens with Tess counting mornings and hoping not to go out; the ending answers that opening by showing her so absorbed in the work that time has stopped mattering. Placed right after the thinning fog and her realization about Warren, the sentence closes the arc of her change. Nothing suggests a scolding, the fog is lifting rather than confusing her, and Warren's only deliberate act in the scene is easing the throttle to give her time.

questions.stem: The main purpose of the passage is to
options: describe how public libraries have expanded into community services, explain why, and weigh the costs of that expansion
argue that libraries should return to lending books and leave social services to other agencies
profile the staff of a single branch library over the course of one Tuesday morning
compare the budgets of library systems in Ohio and Colorado
questions.explanation: The passage opens with the Harlow branch as an example, gives 'two main sources' of the shift in the second and third paragraphs, reports results in the fourth, and then devotes three paragraphs to costs before a balanced closing. The author presents the critics' concerns but ends by noting that most librarians 'would not want' the trend to stop, so the passage weighs rather than argues against the change. Harlow and Larkspur are examples, not the subject.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the first source of the shift in library services was
options: demand from people who brought the library problems they could not bring anywhere else
a decision by professional organizations to redefine the library as a platform
grants that required libraries to hire social workers
a decline in the number of books being checked out
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says 'the first is simply demand' and explains that as other institutions closed, people brought the library questions about benefits, notaries, and collection letters, and 'over time the answers hardened into programs.' The platform idea is identified as the second source, in the next paragraph. Grants are never mentioned, and the decline in circulation is reported as a result, not a cause.

questions.stem: As it is used in the third paragraph, the word 'platform' most nearly means
options: a base of resources on which many different services can be built
a raised stage from which speakers address an audience
a formal statement of an organization's political positions
a software application for searching a catalog
questions.explanation: The paragraph explains that on this view 'the building, the staff, and the public trust' are 'assets that can support almost any public good,' then lists job fairs, tax help, tool lending, and social workers. A platform in this sense is a foundation for many uses. The author notes the word is 'borrowed deliberately from the technology industry,' but the meaning here is the general one of a supporting base, not a specific software product, a stage, or a political platform.

questions.stem: The passage indicates that the Larkspur County library system
options: went from one full-time social worker in 2017 to four by 2024
cut its materials budget by nearly a fifth between 2015 and 2023
holds its busiest hour on Tuesday mornings
reported that its social workers had made three hundred referrals
questions.explanation: The third paragraph states that Larkspur 'hired its first full-time social worker in 2017; by 2024 it had four,' with 'more than three thousand referrals,' not three hundred. The budget cut and the Tuesday morning crowd both belong to the Harlow system in Ohio, which the passage uses as its other example.

questions.stem: The author supports the claim that, 'measured by use, the results are striking' primarily by
options: citing a trend in program attendance and survey findings about how adults view their local library
describing the folding table where a county nurse takes blood pressure readings
quoting librarians who say they did not sign up to be the last public institution standing
reporting that the Harlow system's program budget has more than doubled
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph follows the claim with two kinds of evidence: program attendance 'has grown steadily' while checkouts have declined, and surveys find a majority of adults consider the library important, with higher shares among lower-income people. The nurse's table is scene-setting in the first paragraph, the librarians' complaint appears among the costs, and the doubled program budget measures spending rather than use.

questions.stem: According to the passage, one consequence of the Harlow system's spending changes between 2015 and 2023 was that
options: patrons who come mainly for books, including many older adults and children, noticed the smaller materials budget
the system was forced to close its study room to legal aid volunteers
program attendance at the branch fell for the first time in twenty years
the county stopped sending a nurse to the branch on Tuesdays
questions.explanation: The fifth paragraph reports that the materials budget 'fell by nearly a fifth in real terms while its program budget more than doubled,' and adds that 'patrons who come for the books, a group that still includes a great many older adults and children, have noticed.' The legal aid volunteer and county nurse are still present in the opening scene, and the passage says program attendance has grown, not fallen.

questions.stem: The author includes the remark that some librarians 'did not sign up to be the last public institution standing' primarily in order to
options: voice the staff's view that the library is absorbing work that other agencies ought to be doing
show that librarians are proud to be the only institution still serving the public
argue that libraries should close their doors when other agencies do
explain why library programs have become so popular with patrons
questions.explanation: The remark appears in the paragraph on costs to staff, right after the author notes that new duties 'arrived without new training or pay,' and it is immediately followed by the complaint that treating the library as a safety net 'lets other agencies off the hook for work that is properly theirs.' The sentence is a grievance, not a boast, and the author does not endorse closing libraries or use the remark to explain popularity.

questions.stem: It can reasonably be inferred that the author believes the trend toward community services in libraries
options: is likely to continue, since neither its critics nor most librarians are positioned to stop it
will reverse once materials budgets are restored to earlier levels
has already been rejected by most of the profession
is a temporary response to the closing of other institutions
questions.explanation: The final paragraph states that 'none of these objections has slowed the trend' and that most librarians 'would not want it to,' then observes that 'the people in line at ten on Tuesday morning are not going anywhere.' Together these lines point to a trend the author expects to persist. The choice saying the trend will reverse once budgets are restored is the strongest distractor because budgets are a real concern in the passage, but the author never suggests restored budgets would reverse the shift.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is presented in the passage as a concern or opinion rather than as a reported fact?
options: A library that offers everything to everyone risks standing for nothing in particular.
The Harlow system's materials budget fell by nearly a fifth in real terms between 2015 and 2023.
Program attendance at American public libraries has grown as physical checkouts have declined.
The Larkspur County system reported more than three thousand referrals by its social workers.
questions.explanation: The seventh paragraph introduces the 'everything to everyone' statement as 'a third concern' and attributes the worry about erosion to 'critics,' marking it as a viewpoint. The budget figures, the attendance trend, and the Larkspur referral count are all stated flatly as facts drawn from records, surveys, and reports.
